title.en: The Igigu Rebellion and the Making of Man
title.zh: 伊吉吉叛變與人類之造

region.en: Nippur and the gods' earthworks, Iraq
region.zh: 尼普魯與眾神工程（伊拉克）

texts.period: Old Babylonian, c. 18th c. BCE (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Ea and Atrakhasis', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: The great gods burden the Igigu with digging the rivers for centuries; at last they surround Enlil's temple and refuse the shovel. Enki and the mother goddess knead mankind from clay and the blood of a slain god: the workers who will carry the gods' labor.
summary.zh: 大神令伊吉吉掘河數百年；最後眾神圍恩利爾神殿、罷鏟不掘。恩基與母神以黏土及被誅神之血揉合成人——承擔神之勞役的工眾誕生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: For centuries the Igigu dig the rivers, dredge canals and pile the earthworks; their strength is spent, their hands too heavy. At last they surround the house of Enlil, god of force and judgment, and refuse the shovel: who will take the burden?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet I (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Enlil's fear is calmed by wise Ea's counsel: a god must die for the new work. One of the Igigu — We-ila — is slain, and Nintu the mother goddess kneads clay with his blood; on the tenth day the seventh man is formed: mankind, made to carry the gods' baskets.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet I, creation scene; not verbatim.

functions: Founding myth of human labor as divine service
Etiology of the temple corvee economy
Theology of the strike: labor dispute as cosmogony

variants.name: Enuma Elish: man from Qingu's blood
variants.summary: The Babylonian epic's version of the same creation.

variants.name: Enki and Ninmah
variants.summary: The Sumerian prototype of the clay creation.

texts.canonical_translation: Robert W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 1912

primary_sources.citation: Tablet I, trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912), Old Babylonian recension

texts.period: Old Babylonian, c. 18th c. BCE (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Ea and Atrakhasis', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Six hundred years later the land teems and the people's noise again disturbs Enlil; he sends pestilence. Atrahasis, told by Ea to stop worshipping all gods but Namtara, starves the god of death out — the plague ceases: mankind survives by giving Namtara bread and water.
summary.zh: 六百年後人丁鼎盛，喧囂再擾恩利爾；他降下瘟疫。埃亞授計阿特拉哈西斯：專祭死神納姆塔爾、斷絕他神之祭；死神因饑而求和——瘟疫止息：人類以麵包與水救了自己。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Six hundred years of teeming births later, the land roars with people like a wild ox, and Enlil, troubled by their noise, sends Namtara to destroy them: let pestilence make an end of the clamor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet I-II (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ea instructs Atrahasis: worship every god but Namtara — starve the death-god out. Atrahasis gathers the people, and the offerings to Namtara alone bring him bread and water; the god, shamed, accepts the first offering in six centuries and the plague ceases.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet I-II; not verbatim.

functions: Myth of ritual bargaining with the god of death

variants.name: Atrahasis: the famine
variants.summary: The second and third trials of the same poem.

primary_sources.citation: Tablets I-II, trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

title.en: Famine and Drought: The Second and Third Trials
title.zh: 饑荒與乾旱：第二三次災劫

texts.period: Old Babylonian, c. 18th c. BCE (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Ea and Atrakhasis', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Enlil tries again: Adad withholds the rain, the earth's produce fails, year after year the famine eats deeper — mothers sell children — until Ea's counsel has mankind worship Adad alone, and the rain god relents.
summary.zh: 恩利爾再施毒計：阿達德收雨，地產枯竭，年復一年饑荒日深——母親賣兒——直至埃亞授計，人們獨祭阿達德；雨神心軟降雨。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; famine imagery belongs to the mythic register.

passages.text: Enlil tries again: Adad withholds his rain, Tiamat's fields crack, the year's produce fails; a second year brings dust, a third famine's depth — mothers barter their children for food, houses are closed, the land is a grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet II (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Again Ea's counsel: worship Adad alone. The rain god, faced with the starving altar, relents and sends the rains — mankind, saved a second time by the wise man's management of divine needs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet II; not verbatim.

functions: Myth of famine as divine management crisis

variants.name: Atrahasis: the flood
variants.summary: The final trial of the poem.

primary_sources.citation: Tablet II, trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

title.zh: 阿特拉哈西斯與大洪水

region.zh: 幼發拉底河畔舒魯帕克（伊拉克）

texts.period: Old Babylonian, c. 18th c. BCE (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Ea and Atrakhasis', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Enlil resolves on the flood; Ea, speaking through a reed wall, orders Atrahasis to build the boat, load his household and the beasts, and seal it. Seven days the storm drowns the land; the sacrifice on the mountain draws the hungry gods like flies.
summary.zh: 恩利爾決意滅世；埃亞隔葦牆傳令：造舟、載家眷與百獸、封口。風暴七日淹沒大地；山上之祭使飢餓的諸神如蠅聚集。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enlil resolves to destroy mankind; Ea, forbidden to warn, speaks through the reed wall of Atrahasis's house: Wall, hear; reed wall, understand — tear down your house and build a boat, load it with your household and the seed of all living, and seal the door.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet III (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The storm floods the land for seven days; the boat rides the waves. Atrahasis opens the window, offers sacrifice on the mountain, and the gods, starving since the world's people died, gather like flies to the sweet smell — and Enlil, appeased, decrees a new order with fertility limited so the clamor will not return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet III; not verbatim.

functions: Master narrative of the flood tradition
Etiology of fertility limitations and birth rites
Charter of the wise man's covenant with heaven

variants.summary: The flood retold inside the epic of Gilgamesh.

title.en: Barren Women and the Demon Pashittu

texts.period: Old Babylonian, c. 18th c. BCE (Rogers translation 1912)

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Ea and Atrakhasis', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Enlil's peace is made with a regulated womb: Nintu creates the barren woman, the demoness Pashittu who snatches infants, and the classes of priestesses who may not bear — and the birth rites are instituted, so the clamor never returns.
summary.zh: 恩利爾以受控之生育締和：寧圖造不育之婦、奪嬰之魔帕什圖、不可生育的祭司階層——並定產褥之禮，喧囂自此不復。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Enlil's peace includes a regulated womb: Nintu creates the barren woman who will not bear, and the demoness Pashittu who snatches infants from their mothers' laps.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet III end (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The birth rites are instituted: the mat of the birth-stool, the brick of the laboring woman, the offerings that mark the days after delivery — the poem closes with these settlements, the flood's price fixed in ritual.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Atrahasis, Tablet III end; not verbatim.

functions: Charter of birth rites and fertility regulation

variants.name: Lamashtu demonology
variants.summary: The developed cult of the infant-snatching demoness.

primary_sources.citation: Tablet III, closing sections, trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

title.zh: 克蘇特魯斯：貝羅蘇斯洪水記

texts.period: Berossus' Babyloniaca, c. 290 BCE, preserved in George Smith 1876

source.work: The Chaldean Account of Genesis, George Smith (1876), ch. on Berossus

summary.en: The god Cronus warns Xisuthrus in a dream that a flood will destroy mankind, and to bury the writings at Sippar and build the boat; the flood passes, birds are sent out, and the survivor descends with his family — translating the Babylonian deluge into Greek chronicle.
summary.zh: 克羅諾斯神於夢中警告克蘇特魯斯：洪水將滅人類，命其於西帕爾埋藏典籍、建造大舟。洪水退後放鳥試探，倖存者攜家眷下舟——巴比倫洪水敘事經希臘史家之筆傳世。

sensitivity.note: Hellenistic retelling; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The god Cronus appears to Xisuthrus in a dream and warns him: on the fifteenth day of the month Daisios mankind shall be destroyed by a flood; bury the beginnings and endings of all things at Sippar, and build the boat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Berossus' flood account as given in George Smith, Chaldean Account of Genesis (1876); not verbatim.

passages.text: The flood passes; birds are sent out and return without a place to rest until the third bird does not return. Xisuthrus descends with wife, daughter and pilot, pays worship to the gods, and vanishes with them; the company left in the boat searches and hears a voice from the air — go down to Babylon and dig up the writings at Sippar, and hand them to mankind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Berossus' account (1876); not verbatim.

functions: Late transmission of the flood myth to the classical world
Charter of the buried scriptures motif
texts.canonical_translation: George Smith, The Chaldean Account of Genesis, 1876

primary_sources.citation: as quoted in George Smith, The Chaldean Account of Genesis (1876), Berossus chapter

secondary_sources.citation: Donald A. Mackenzie, London, 1915, ch. on the deluge
